newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus rises for first time in 2 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus rises for first time in 2 yrs.

text.p: Japan's trade surplus rose last month for the first time in two years, confounding expectations of a hefty drop, as the weaker yen fuelled a spurt in exports, particularly of cars.

The marginal rise in the surplus, announced by the Finance Ministry on Wednesday, took economists by surprise and pointed to the possibility of the changing trade pattern boosting the yen against the dollar and stoking up trade tension.

The customs-cleared trade surplus clicked up 0.2 percent to 675.19 billion yen ($5.92 billion). But the politically sensitive surplus with the United States leapt more than 30 percent, due mainly to a surge in car exports.
"It's quite a surprise. It's the first increase in the surplus for two years. It's certainly higher than we expected," said Richard Jerram, ING Baring Securities chief economist in Tokyo.
"Certainly, if anything, it shows the trade surplus is going to be turning around earlier than we expected."

A Reuter poll of economists ahead of the data had predicted a 28 percent drop in the overall surplus. Although the yen's fall from record highs against the dollar last year has put the brakes on the progressive fall in Japan's trade surplus, economists had not been expecting an actual rise quite so soon.

Economists said the yen, which has fallen steadily this year from around 105 to the dollar in January, could strengthen again over time if a rising surplus becomes an established trend. Strong exports mean Japanese firms have more dollar earnings to convert into yen.

The dollar slipped on the widening trade gap, standing at around 113.50 yen in morning trade against a late Friday U.S. level of around 113.85 yen. The surprise reversal of the trade trend also weighed on Tokyo stocks, as a stronger yen would hurt Japanese exporters.
The surplus with the United States surged 31.2 percent in November from a year earlier to 378.39 billion yen ($3.31 billion).

A Finance Ministry official said the key factor behind this was a 45.7 percent surge in car exports to the United States, while a fall in aircraft imports also contributed to the rise in the overall surplus. A weaker yen makes Japanese products cheaper in terms of foreign currency.
But the official said the general trend in the trade surplus remained downward and some private economists agreed.
"I doubt if Japan's trade surplus will keep rising," said Shigekiko Mori, an economist at DKB Research Institute. "There is a possibility that the surplus will show a decline again."
"There will not be a change in the business structure of Japanese companies in which they have shifted production abroad," Mori added.
Others, however, warned that the sudden reversal heralded a possible return of trade friction with the United States and a shift in U.S. authorities' stance in favour of a strong dollar.

"The U.S. government will start applying some pressure on the Japanese...so the yen's basic trend will be stronger than the current level, that means maybe below 110 yen," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute.

"At the moment there doesn't seem to be any great pressure (for the U.S.) to take out a big stick and beat Japan on trade, but if the surplus keeps on going up, I'm sure in the New Year you will see a more aggressive stance," ING Baring's Jerram said. ($1=114 yen)
